Bell’s palsy Bell’s palsy is a condition that may be caused1,2 by herpes simplex virus 1. It affects the facial nerves and results in facial muscle weakness and paralysis. It is often accompa- nied by pain and lachrymation. Untreated, over 80% of all patients recover completely or almost so, while in a small- er number facial weakness persists; complete failure of motor recovery is very rare. Corticosteroids dramatically relieve pain associated with Bell’s palsy,3 and their use in treatment is widely accept- ed.4 The suggested oral dose of prednisone for adults is 1 mg/kg daily in divided doses morning and evening; if the paralysis remains incomplete after 5 or 6 days the pred- nisone is gradually withdrawn over the next 5 days but if the paralysis is complete the initial dosage should be con- tinued for another 10 days and then gradually withdrawn.3 While a review of 4 studies in 1996 suggested an increased rate of complete recovery with corticosteroid treatment,5 and others consider treatment to decrease the incidence of permanent facial paralysis,2 not all studies have shown such benefits.2,6 The original review included a study in which a large number of patients were lost to follow-up, and a more recent review concluded that available evi- dence does not show significant benefit from corticoster- oid therapy,6 although their anti-inflammatory effects might prevent nerve damage. There is some suggestion that addition of aciclovir or valaciclovir to corticosteroid treatment may improve outcome,4,7 although again sub- stantive evidence is lacking.2,8 1. Murakami S, et al.
